description: We’re TideX 🌊 — a team using NASA Earth observation data and AI to tackle real-world environmental challenges in Oman. We’re working on an early-warning solution for harmful algal blooms and their impact on desalination plants.If you enjoy building innovative solutions and turning data into real-world impact, join us!
summary:
The Gulf countries run around 40% of the world's desalination capacity, and here in Oman about 86% of our drinking water comes from desalinated seawater. So when something goes wrong in the sea, it hits our taps directly. In late 2008 a red tide reached the coast near Muscat and the Barka plant had to shut down for 55 days. The plants only found out when the algae was already at their intakes.

We built TideX to give them that warning earlier. It uses NASA satellite data (MODIS-Aqua chlorophyll and sea temperature) and looks for spots where chlorophyll jumps well above what is normal for that area. Then it measures how far each bloom is from six desalination plants along our coast. We also added NASA OSCAR ocean currents, so the app can tell if a bloom is drifting toward a plant or away from it, and roughly when it will arrive. Everything shows on a map in Arabic and English, and operators can download a PDF report.

To test it, we went back to the real 2008 data. TideX would have flagged the bloom near Barka on 22 October, while it only reached the coast on 16 November. That is 25 days the plant could have used to prepare.
details:
What it does

TideX is a web dashboard that warns desalination plants when a harmful algal bloom (red tide) is getting close to their seawater intake. It reads NASA satellite data, finds bloom areas, and shows how far each one is from every plant. We set it up for six plants on the coast of Oman (Al Ghubrah, Barka, Sohar, Sur, Duqm and Salalah). A plant is marked "warning" when a bloom is within 50 km and "critical" when it is within 20 km.

How it works

We use MODIS-Aqua chlorophyll-a as the main signal. A bloom is flagged when chlorophyll is at least 3 mg/m3 and about three times higher than that same spot's normal level over the previous 30 days. We only keep patches larger than about 640 km2, and we skip the pixels right next to the coast because turbid water there gives false readings. After that, NASA OSCAR surface currents tell us which way each bloom is drifting and roughly how many hours or days it needs to reach each plant.

Testing on real NASA data from 2008

We did not stop at a demo. We downloaded the real satellite archive for the 2008 red tide in the Sea of Oman, the event that shut down the Barka plant for 55 days:

- MODIS-Aqua daily chlorophyll-a, Level-3, 4 km (NASA OB.DAAC), 92 days from 1 October to 31 December 2008

- MODIS-Aqua daily sea surface temperature, Level-3, 4 km (NASA OB.DAAC), same 92 days

- OSCAR surface currents, version 2.0, 0.25 degree (NASA PO.DAAC), for the key days of the crisis

Running TideX day by day on this data, it flagged a bloom 35 km from Barka on 22 October, and the bloom reached the coast on 16 November. That is 25 days of warning. On 22 October the currents were pushing the bloom away, so TideX showed "warning, moving away" instead of a false alarm, and that is what actually happened. On 15 November it estimated the bloom would reach Barka in about 20 hours, and it arrived the next day.

Benefits and impact

More than 300 million people around the world depend on desalinated water, and the Gulf alone runs around 40% of the world's desalination capacity. Red tides are becoming more frequent in the Gulf, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean, California, Chile and East Asia, and a single bloom can stop a plant and damage its RO membranes. TideX can work on any coastline: you only change the list of plants and the map area. It runs on free NASA data, so even a small water utility in a developing country can use it without paying for satellite services. Having days of warning instead of hours means operators can adjust pre-treatment, clean filters, fill storage tanks and keep water flowing to whole cities.

What is new in TideX

- It links ocean satellite data directly to specific plants and turns it into a distance and an arrival time, not just a colored map.

- It detects blooms by comparing each spot with its own normal level, so waters that are naturally green do not trigger false alarms.

- It uses ocean currents to tell whether a bloom is coming or going, which cuts down false alarms.

- It was tested on a real crisis (2008) using real NASA data, not only a simulation.

- It is easy to use: one page, a date slider, color alerts (red, yellow, green), Arabic and English, and a one-click PDF report for managers. An operator does not need any background in satellites or coding.

Tools

Python, Streamlit, Plotly, Xarray, NetCDF4, NumPy, Pandas, SciPy and fpdf2. NASA data was downloaded through Earthdata using the earthaccess library.

Challenges we faced

- Our first method simply looked for high chlorophyll, and it gave false alarms everywhere, especially in the Arabian Sea after the monsoon and close to the shore. We had to rethink the approach and move to the anomaly method with patch size filtering.

- NASA files are global and large, so we wrote scripts that download each day and cut out only Omani waters. Downloading everything on a mobile connection was also a challenge.

- Clouds hide the sea surface on many days, so we fill the gaps with the average of the last few days.

- Getting Arabic text to display correctly in the PDF report took a lot of trial and error with fonts and right-to-left layout.

- We had to match three datasets with different grids (chlorophyll at 4 km, currents at 25 km) and different file formats.

- Time: we built, tested and fixed everything within the hackathon window.

What is next

Chlorophyll alone cannot tell harmful algae from harmless ones. Next we want to use NASA PACE hyperspectral data to identify the algae type, add automatic daily downloads, and send alerts by SMS or email.

Acknowledgements and local expertise

We did not rely on online sources only. We consulted faculty from the Department of Marine Science and Fisheries, College of Agricultural and Marine Sciences at Sultan Qaboos University, who helped us understand red tide species in the Sea of Oman, the 2008-2009 bloom, and how blooms affect desalination intakes. We also used textbooks from the SQU library for background on harmful algal blooms and remote sensing of chlorophyll. We also visited desalination plants and asked the staff about this problem. They confirmed that red tides are a real problem they deal with, that a bloom lowers the quality of the raw seawater coming into the plant, and that this directly affects the desalination process. This is exactly the gap TideX tries to close.

Use of AI tools

We used an AI assistant (Claude) to help write and debug parts of the Python code and data scripts, and to help produce the pitch video graphics and subtitles. The idea, the 2008 case study, the NASA data choices and the narration are our own.
